overview: Early medieval Frisian communities lived along the southern North Sea, linking farms on raised mounds with coastal trade and powerful leaders. This card concerns the map’s 600 to 800 period, not every earlier or later group called Frisian. Its outline simplifies a changing network of communities and political influence.

periods.title: Coastal leaders and connections
periods.summary: Redbad became a formidable rival and occasional partner of the Franks.

periods.title: Gradual Frankish conquest
periods.summary: Conquest proceeded in stages, including western Friesland in 734 and eastern regions later in the century.

sections.title: Putting the house above the water

items.text: Coastal people built artificial dwelling mounds called terps because the salt marshes could flood. Small house mounds could grow or merge into larger village mounds. Staying dry meant adapting the ground beneath the home, an engineering solution maintained across many generations.

Manure and household rubbish helped form the layers of terp soil. Much later, people quarried that rich earth as fertiliser, exposing ancient objects and buildings. Archaeologists now study surviving layers to separate centuries of rebuilding, waste disposal and everyday occupation.

The early seventh-century Wijnaldum brooch contains more than 300 pieces of red garnet. Researchers traced the stones probably to India, reaching the North Sea through long-distance exchange. The ornament was assembled from materials whose journeys stretched far beyond the wearer’s home.

Researchers now associate this splendid brooch with a high-status woman, rather than automatically with a king. Its fragments were recovered over decades and fitted together like a difficult puzzle. Her name is unknown, but the object preserves extraordinary craftsmanship and access to valuable materials.

Dorestad on the Rhine was a busy international market around 800, during the Frankish period. Ships linked it with western European trade routes. This harbour belonged to the broader commercial world used by coastal communities, rather than proving that an independent Frisian king still ruled there.

Dorestad’s inhabitants included ship operators and craftspeople making goods for exchange. Excavators recovered ordinary utensils alongside weapons and rich jewellery. The waterfront’s prosperity depended on many kinds of labour, not only the merchants whose transactions made the place famous.

Archaeobotanical research shows a long tradition of growing barley and horse beans on northern salt marshes. Modern experimental plots help researchers test how such crops cope with salty ground. These trials reveal practical possibilities; they are not a record of one medieval family’s harvest.

The man buried at Bernuthsfeld around 700 wore a woollen garment assembled from 45 reused pieces of cloth. His clothes survived in the bog. Careful reuse could involve a remarkable amount of sewing, although the patches alone do not establish whether he was poor.

The bog also preserved hair and bones, allowing later study with techniques including CT scanning. The surviving clothing gives unusually direct evidence of how fabric was put together. It is one individual’s outfit, so we should not dress every Frisian in an identical patchwork tunic.

Politics could involve family relationships as well as fighting. Redbad’s daughter Theudesinde married Grimoald, son of the Frankish leader Pepin. Such marriages connected powerful households even when the surrounding kingdoms competed fiercely for territory and influence.

An antler comb found at Oostum carries runes. One published reading includes “cabu”, meaning “comb”. This is a Roman-letter transliteration of the carved word, not the original letter shapes. The object is broadly dated to 700 to 950, so it may belong after the map’s endpoint.

One interpretation has Habuku making the comb for Aib; another reverses those roles. Writing here accompanies personal grooming and skilled craft. It brings us much closer to an individual object than to a royal proclamation.

ending.text: Frankish rulers absorbed Frisian territories in stages during the eighth century. Political independence changed, while coastal settlements and Frisian identities continued. The year 800 is the imported map endpoint, not the end of the people.
